title: A Journey North
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 13 of 40
content:
The journey north began with a borrowed cart, two tea chests, and a map Iroh insisted was more accurate than it looked.

“The map is upside down,” I said.

“It is not.”

“The river is labeled above the mountains.”

“Perhaps the mountains have moved.”

“You are the worst navigator I have ever met.”

“You have traveled with very impressive navigators.”

“I have traveled with people who could read.”

Iroh turned the map around. “A minor adjustment.”

The cart rolled through the outer districts of Ba Sing Se and onto the road. The city walls receded behind me. For the first time since arriving, I could see open land without a gate or tower interrupting the horizon.

Iroh had been asked to help negotiate with several former military governors. He had decided to carry tea as well as official letters.

“Why bring the tea?” I asked.

“People say more truthful things while waiting for water to boil.”

“That sounds like an unreliable diplomatic method.”

“It has a better success rate than shouting.”

I sat beside him on the cart. The road was uneven. Every rut moved my shoulder against his.

“You could have gone alone,” I said.

“I could have.”

“Why didn’t you?”

He kept his eyes on the road. “Because I wanted you with me.”

The answer warmed me more than the sun.

“That’s not the same as needing me,” I said.

“No.”

“Good.”

“I am learning the distinction.”

The first village welcomed Iroh with suspicion. The governor had not arrived. The tea house had no spare room. I and Iroh slept in a storage shed after sweeping out a family of mice.

“They were here first,” Iroh said.

“You are defending the mice?”

“I respect their persistence.”

I sat on a rolled blanket while he brewed tea over a small brazier. The shed smelled of dust and dried herbs.

“This is not what I imagined,” I said.

“The journey is often rude about our expectations.”

“You make everything sound like a lesson.”

“You make everything sound like an accusation.”

“You are enjoying this.”

“Immensely.”

The governor arrived the next morning with six guards and an expression that suggested he had not slept well in years. Iroh invited him to tea. The meeting lasted three hours.

I served cups. I watched the governor's hands. He drank too quickly whenever Iroh mentioned disarmament.

“The army protected this region,” the governor said.

“It also ruled it through fear,” Iroh replied.

“Fear kept order.”

“So does a locked door. That does not make it a home.”

The governor's face reddened.

I expected Iroh to push harder. Instead, he poured another cup.

“What are you afraid will happen if your soldiers leave?” Iroh asked.

The question changed the room.

The governor looked toward the window. He spoke of bandits, rival provinces, and people who would take advantage of weakness. Underneath every argument was the fear of being responsible for a place without an army to blame.

Iroh listened.

By sunset, the governor had agreed to send half his soldiers home and allow an independent council to form.

“That is not a complete victory,” I said while packing the tea chests.

“No.”

“You look pleased.”

“A small change made honestly is more valuable than a large promise made for applause.”

I loaded the last chest. Iroh's hand brushed mine.

“You were good in there,” I said.

“I drank tea.”

“You asked the question nobody else wanted to ask.”

“Questions can be doors.”

“You have used that line before.”

“It remains useful.”

The road turned north into hills. The air cooled. Pine trees replaced fields. Iroh wrapped a second cloak around my shoulders without comment.

“I can dress myself,” I said.

“I know.”

“Then why?”

“Because you are cold.”

“You could have asked.”

“Would you have said no?”

“Possibly.”

“Then I would have respected it.”

The words made me stop walking.

Iroh looked back. “What is it?”

“You are getting better at saying things before you do them.”

“I am practicing.”

I stepped closer. “Can I kiss you?”

He smiled. “You may.”

The path was empty. The cart waited farther ahead. I kissed him between the pines, his cloak around my shoulders, the scent of smoke and tea clinging to him.

His hands rested at my back. When I pressed closer, he made a low, surprised sound.

“The road is watching,” he murmured.

“The road has seen worse.”

“It is very judgmental.”

“You say that about telescopes and roads.”

“They are related.”

I laughed against his mouth.

That night, I camped beside a stream. Iroh cooked rice with mushrooms. It was simple and good. He told me stories of traveling with his nephew, careful enough to make Zuko sound like a person rather than a legend.

“He is doing his best,” Iroh said.

“So are you.”

“Yes.”

“Does that make it easier?”

“No. It makes it worth doing.”

The fire crackled between us. Stars appeared above the trees.

I reached across the blanket. Iroh took my hand.

The road north continued in the morning.

For now, the two of us slept beneath the same sky.

The journey continued through villages that had been ignored by every capital they had ever served. People brought Iroh lists of missing relatives, broken irrigation tools, unpaid debts, and disputes that had grown into feuds because no official had listened.

He listened to all of them.

Sometimes, he could help. Sometimes, he could only write a name in a book and promise to carry it to someone with authority. He never promised a result merely because people wanted comfort.

I learned to recognize the look on his face when the promise was beyond his power. His jaw tightened. His eyes went distant. His hands became very still.

“You are doing it,” I told him one evening.

“Doing what?”

“Trying to carry every name.”

the two of us sat beside a field while the horses grazed. The sky was violet.

Iroh closed the notebook. “If I do not remember them, who will?”

“They have families.”

“Some do not.”

“Then write the names. Do not become the names.”

He looked at me.

“You cannot help anyone if you turn yourself into a memorial,” I continued.

Iroh's gaze dropped to the notebook.

“That was harsh,” I said.

“It was precise.”

“You are allowed to disagree.”

“I am considering it.”

“Dangerous.”

“Very.”

He opened the notebook again and placed it in his bag.

“What do you do when you cannot fix something?” he asked.

“I pretend I can until someone tells me to stop.”

“That is not a healthy answer.”

“I did not say it was.”

He reached for my hand. “Then perhaps we should learn together.”

The next village had no tea house. I brewed tea beneath a tree while Iroh met with the council. A child watched me measure leaves.

“Is it magic?” she asked.

“No. It is practice.”

“Can I try?”

I handed her the spoon. She poured too much.

“That is too many,” I said.

“How do you know?”

“Because Iroh will make a face when he drinks it.”

The child giggled.

When Iroh returned, I served him the tea. He took a sip and made a solemn expression.

“It is powerful,” he said.

The child beamed.

“It is also very bitter,” he added.

“You cannot say both.”

“I can. It is an important diplomatic skill.”

The child asked him whether he was a dragon. Iroh said that he had been called one. She asked whether dragons liked tea.

“Some do,” he said.

“Do you?”

“Very much.”

She looked at me. “Do you love him?”

I choked on my tea.

Iroh's eyes widened.

The child waited with the ruthless patience of someone too young to understand embarrassment.

“Yes,” I said.

Iroh's expression softened.

“He loves you too,” the child decided.

“That is a conclusion,” Iroh said.

“Is it wrong?”

“No.”

The child returned to her family. I stared at the cup in my hands.

“You could have answered,” I said.

“I wanted to hear you say it.”

“You already heard me.”

“I enjoy repetition.”

I kissed him beside the tree.

The road through the hills was difficult, but the days became full of small kindnesses: sharing fruit, repairing wheels, making tea for strangers, and sleeping beneath open skies.

I did not save everyone.

I did not need to.

I helped where I could, and We returned to the cart together.

At night, Iroh placed the notebook between us instead of hiding it in his bag.

“You may read,” he said.

“Only if you want me to.”

“I want you to know what I am carrying.”

I did not open it. I placed my hand over the cover.

“Then I will sit with it,” I said.

Iroh covered my hand with his.

The notebook remained closed, but the distance between us grew smaller.

In the morning, Iroh brewed tea without being asked. I carried the cups to the cart.

The tea was strong.

It warmed the morning.

So did his smile.

The cart waited beneath the tree.
